name: Emirate of Sicily
info: The Islamic state of Sicily, conquered from the Byzantine Empire by the Aghlabids of Ifriqiya and later ruled by the Kalbid emirs, a prosperous Mediterranean power with Palermo as its capital.

facts.founder: The Aghlabid dynasty of Ifriqiya, whose conquest was led by the qadi Asad ibn al-Furat; al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Kalbi was the first Kalbid emir

t: The Aghlabid conquest of Sicily began with a landing at Mazara del Vallo in 827 and took Palermo in 831, but the island was not fully conquered until Taormina fell in 902.
From 948 the Kalbid dynasty ruled Sicily as autonomous emirs while formally acknowledging the Fatimid caliphs.
Arab rule brought land reforms, qanat irrigation and new crops such as oranges, lemons, pistachio and sugarcane.
dyk: Ibn Hawqal, a Baghdad merchant who visited Palermo in 950, reckoned 7,000 butchers trading in 150 shops in the city.
ev: Aghlabid forces under Asad ibn al-Furat land at Mazara del Vallo and win the first battle on 15 July
Palermo falls in September after a year-long siege and becomes the Muslim capital of Sicily
The conquest of the island is completed with the fall of Taormina
The Fatimid caliph al-Mansur appoints al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Kalbi governor, the first emir of the Kalbid dynasty
A Christian army under Emperor Otto II is defeated at Stilo, but Emir Abu'l-Qasim is killed in the battle
Under al-Hasan al-Samsam the island breaks into four qadits
Butera, Noto and Malta, the last Arab strongholds, fall to the Normans

sections.foundation:
Sicily had been reconquered for the Roman Empire by Justinian I in 535 and was a peripheral Byzantine province when Muslim forces from Ifriqiya began raiding it in 652. Syracuse was taken in 740, but a Berber revolt forced the invaders home. In 826 Euphemius, commander of the Byzantine fleet of Sicily, rebelled after Emperor Michael II ordered his nose cut off for forcing a nun to marry him. Driven out, he offered the island to Ziyadat Allah, the Aghlabid emir of Ifriqiya.

The conquest was entrusted to the 70-year-old qadi Asad ibn al-Furat, with 10,000 infantry, 700 cavalry and 100 ships. They landed at Mazara del Vallo and won the first battle on 15 July 827. Plague killed Asad during the siege of Syracuse, and Euphemius died at Castrogiovanni. In 830 30,000 Ifriqiyan and Andalusi troops arrived, and in September 831 Palermo fell after a year-long siege. It became the Muslim capital, renamed al-Madinah, "The City". The conquest was a see-saw affair: Messina fell in 842 or 843, Syracuse in 878 and Taormina in 902, while Rometta held out until 965.
sections.socioeconomy:
The new Arab rulers carried out land reforms that ended the dominance of the large estates and encouraged smallholdings. They improved irrigation with qanats and introduced lucrative crops, including oranges, lemons, pistachio and sugarcane, as well as vegetables, dates and mulberry trees where only wheat had been grown for centuries, and mining began. The coins were the gold dinar of 4.25 grams and the silver dirhem of 2.97 grams.

Palermo was a major cultural and political centre of the Muslim world. Ibn Hawqal, who visited in 950, described the walled Kasr with its great Friday Mosque and the suburb of al-Khalisa (Kalsa) with the Sultan's palace, baths, government offices and a prison. Its population is uncertain: Paul Bairoch estimated 350,000 in the 11th century, Stephan R. Epstein closer to 60,000, Kenneth Meyer Setton between 100,000 and 250,000. The island became multiconfessional and multilingual, an Arab-Byzantine culture of Arab and Berber migrants and Latin, Greek and Jewish communities. Christians and Jews were tolerated as dhimmis but paid the jizya and the kharaj; about half the population was Muslim by the Norman Conquest.
sections.military:
The conquest itself took most of the 9th century, against Byzantine troops backed at Syracuse by a Venetian fleet under Doge Giustiniano Participazio. Messina became a base for campaigns into the Italian mainland. Under the conquest's rules the fighters, the junud, took four-fifths of conquered land as booty and one fifth went to the state, the khums.

Under the Kalbids Taormina was conquered again in 962 and Rometta soon after. Raids into Southern Italy went on into the 11th century, and in 982 a Christian army under the Emperor Otto II and the brothers Landulf and Pandulf was defeated at Stilo near Crotone. In 1038 a Byzantine army under George Maniaces, with a corps of Normans and Varangians including Harald Hardrada, crossed the strait of Messina and took Syracuse, but a Muslim counter-offensive won back all the cities lost. The Normans under Roger de Hauteville then invaded. A small Norman force defeated the Sicilians and North Africans at the Battle of Cerami in 1063, and in 1068 Roger defeated the Zirid Ayyub at the Battle of Misilmeri. Palermo fell on 10 January 1072 after a five-month siege.
sections.governance:
The emir, seated in what is now the Royal Palace in Palermo, held authority over the army, administration, justice and the treasury. He appointed the governors of major cities, the high judges (qadi) and arbitrators for minor disputes (hakam). An assembly of notables, the giamà'a, advised him and sometimes made decisions in his place. The authorities very likely ran a tiraz, an official workshop making silk and other fine fabrics as gifts.

The island was divided into three vals: Val di Mazara in the west, more Islamized and directly administered; Val Demone in the northeast, majority Christian and often in revolt, where government focused on taxes and order; and Val di Noto in the southeast. The Sunni Aghlabids ruled until 909, when the Shiite Fatimids replaced them. Sicilian Muslims, mostly Sunni, resisted the new rulers: the first Fatimid governor was expelled in 912, Ibn Qurhub rebelled until 916, and a revolt of 937 was suppressed only in 941. In 948 the caliph al-Mansur appointed al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Kalbi, and after the Fatimids moved to Egypt in 972–973 they recognized the Kalbids as hereditary emirs.
sections.impact:
Sicily became a prosperous and influential commercial power in the Mediterranean, and the wealth of its new crops and irrigation led to a flourishing of art and science. Palermo, beautified with gardens and public works, was compared with Córdoba; the traveller Ibn Jubair, writing at the end of the 12th century, praised its splendour, its four springs and mosques too many to count, most of them also schools. Sunni refugees from the North African rebellions of 943–947 against the Fatimids settled on the island.

Arabic remained a language of government for at least a century under Norman rule, and Muslim craftsmanship, masonry and administrative skill were sought after. The Norman kingdom under Roger II has been called multi-ethnic and religiously tolerant. Traces of the emirate remain in modern Sicily: minor Arabic influence in the Sicilian language and in place names, and a much larger one in Maltese, which derives from Siculo-Arabic. Other remnants are found in the island's farming methods and crops, its cuisine and its architecture.
sections.decline:
With Emir Yusuf al-Kalbi a period of steady decline began. Under Ahmad ibn Yusuf al-Akhal dynastic conflict grew, with factions of the ruling family allied with the Byzantine Empire or the Zirids, and al-Mu'izz ibn Badis tried and failed to annex the island. In 1044, under al-Hasan al-Samsam, Sicily broke into four qadits: those of Abdallah ibn Mankut, Ibn al-Hawwas, Ibn al-Maklati and Ibn al-Thumna, while Palermo came under a council of sheikhs. Ibn al-Thumna worked closely with the Normans against his rivals, and after his death in 1062 Muslim troops made up the majority of the Hauteville army in Sicily.

A Zirid army under Ali and Ayyub ibn Tamim was beaten at Cerami and Misilmeri and went home. Catania fell in 1071 and Palermo in 1072. Ibn Abbad of Syracuse held out until he died in 1086; Hammud of Castrogiovanni surrendered and converted in 1087, and in 1091 Butera, Noto and Malta fell. Muslims long remained a majority and served at the royal court, but Lombard pogroms began in the 1160s. Frederick II deported about 60,000 Muslims to Lucera in Apulia from 1223, many of them enslaved, and the removal of Islam was complete by the late 1240s.

summary: The Emirate of Sicily was the island's Islamic state, built by the Aghlabid conquest from 827 and ruled from Palermo, from 948 by the Kalbid emirs under Fatimid authority. Its new crops and irrigation made it rich and its culture mixed. It broke into rival qadits in the 1040s and fell to the Normans by 1091.
references: Leonard Chiarelli, A History of Muslim Sicily (Midsea Books, 2018)

pointDescs.831: Palermo falls after a year-long siege and becomes the capital of Muslim Sicily.
pointDescs.842: Messina is besieged and captured in 842 or 843 and becomes a base for campaigns on the mainland.
pointDescs.878: Syracuse, the old Byzantine capital of the island, is captured.
pointDescs.902: The fall of Taormina completes the conquest of the island.
pointDescs.917: Fatimid authority is secured with the surrender of Palermo after years of revolt against the new rulers.
pointDescs.948: The caliph al-Mansur appoints al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Kalbi, the first Kalbid emir.
pointDescs.965: Rometta, the last Byzantine stronghold, falls after Taormina is taken again in 962.
pointDescs.982: A Christian army under Otto II is defeated at Stilo, though Emir Abu'l-Qasim is killed.
pointDescs.998: The reign of Yusuf al-Kalbi ends, in a period of steady decline.
pointDescs.1038: A Byzantine army under George Maniaces lands and takes Syracuse before a Muslim counter-offensive.
pointDescs.1044: The island breaks into four rival qadits under al-Hasan al-Samsam.
pointDescs.1063: The Normans win the Battle of Cerami and secure the north-east.
pointDescs.1072: Palermo falls to the Normans on 10 January after a five-month siege.
pointDescs.1086: Syracuse surrenders after the death of Ibn Abbad.
pointDescs.1091: Butera, Noto and Malta, the last Arab strongholds, fall to the Christians.
